en: You need 200 points to guess both dice rolls.
You can bet on what number will show on one of the two dice. If you guess right, you can earn even more chips by simply guessing odd or even.
However, you must wager 20 percent of the betting limit in order to make your bet.

When playing against the house, you will guess either odd or even. Guess right, and your winnings become your bet against the house. You will then guess odd or even again. If you guess right, you win twice the amount of chips you bet. Up to five rolls are possible.
In this game, you try to guess what the difference will be between the two dice. If you guess right, your payout will be your bet multiplied by the difference between the two dice.
Cho-han is a dice-rolling game where you guess if the total value of a pair of dice will be odd or even.

Virtua Fighter 2 is a fighting game. Use the joystick and punch (P), kick (K), and guard (G) to bring your opponent's health to 0 and defeat them.
After winning two rounds against one opponent, you will be able to fight the next one. If you lose two rounds, it's game over.

Each player character has their unique abilities. You can see which button combinations produce which basic abilities by pressing <Action:Button_Touchpad@VirtuaFigter_1P> during play. There are more abilities than just those, though!

Whenever I come through Nagasugai, it's always so busy. It really does live up to its title as one of the biggest cities in the country.
Yeah. There's never a time when folks aren't around.
How come y'wound up working here, Kiryu-san?
How indeed.
I traveled through many cities, but it was here that I ran into someone who found me a place to get settled.
Wow, really? Looks like I gotta give this someone my thanks, then. If not for them, I never woulda met ya, Kiryu-san!
Yes. But after living here for this long, I feel like I fit right in. I might have ended up settling down here even without his help.
Ya don't say? What's it y'like about this place, anyhow?
The scenery is beautiful, for one. Being situated between two rivers like this is quite unusual, as far as big cities go.
I know, right? I'm really fond of the sights here in Nagasu, too.
If it was just about lookin' pretty, the area 'round the train station would be considered nice too. But there ain't nowhere in Hakata quite like this.
Back when I lived in Okinawa, I felt the same way about the ocean. A good environment is calming. It's ideal for healing a wounded soul.
Does that mean you're gonna stay livin' here in Hakata forever and ever?
Who knows what tomorrow will bring? It's hard to say anything is certain.
There are lots of pretty girls. That's reason enough right there, don't you think?
Hehe. Aw, ain't nobody gonna decide where to live just 'cause of that!
But wouldn't you rather live in a town full of studs over one full of losers?
Nah, I ain't like that. I'm not the kinda person to judge a book by its cover, y'know?
A good heart is better than good looks, every time. Y'only really know a guy after you've spent a whole lotta time with him.
Looks like you'll need to get to know me a lot better, too.
Hehe. Sure thing!
The food's delicious. It might even be the best in the whole country.
I guess it is pretty tasty. But I've never lived anywhere else, so I'm thinkin' I wouldn't really know anyhow.
Is the food in other cities really not as good?
It's not bad, per se. But when it comes to local delicacies and specialty foods, Hakata's are some of the most popular in all of Japan.
I bet if you ever went somewhere else, it wouldn't be long before you'd miss the food here.
Hm. I do gotta wonder. Maybe I might really like it if I tried somethin' from someplace new, y'know?
Maybe so. You should plan a cross-country trip and try as many foods as you can.
Ah, that sounds great!
It really is quite cold outside.
Maybe yer feelin' it more because you're used to bein' cooped up inside. You oughta get outside and walk more.
No way! I do most of my walking underground, anyway.
Underground? Oh, right. The underground shoppin' mall.
Yeah! There are a whole bunch of shops here under Tsukimino! We could give Kamurocho a run for its money!
I haven't been down there yet. Is it really that big?
It is. The underground walkways stretch all the way from Sapporo Station to Tsukimino Station. So there's no need to walk out in the open air!
Sounds big. Glad I didn't go there then. If I did, I'm sure I woulda gotten lost.
It's fine! Tsukimino is all one giant grid, and the underground is basically the same. You won't lose your way as long as you know your location.
A grid, huh? Like Kyoto, then. I could probably handle that.
It's really handy, because so long as you know the address, you can find a place no problem. Even if you've never been there before!
But don't ya get mixed up 'cause all of the buildings look the same? It's good to have a little variety in yer city, too.
I suppose so. But don't you think the Tsukimino intersection is a pretty big landmark?
True. They've got those big ol' signs, so it stands out.
It's prettier outside. Walkin' underground is a wasted opportunity.
No, the underground is pretty! It's got this kind of near-future thing going on. The lighting and whatnot is very chic.
Hmph, I'm not interested in that sorta thing. I don't give a damn about some place that's all cold and lifeless. It's borin'.
What? But Tsukimino is made up of rows of buildings that all look the same, too. Isn't  that just as boring?
Ain't every day you see the town blanketed in snow. Almost never happens in Kamurocho or Sotenbori.
I see. Snow's nothing special for me, but I guess it's rare for people outside Sapporo.
I thought I'd get sick of seein' it over the last two years, but guess I haven't.
Just take the train. No reason else they'd have all these tracks everywhere.
But it's not just a regular underground tunnel. There are stores lined up all along the way, perfect for grabbing a meal or doing some shopping.
Most large buildings have underground floors that are connected too, so you can get around fine without ever having to go outside.
Yeah, but when I'm under Kamurocho, I dunno what leads where. Why's everything between these stations even connected?
Ah, I get you! You exit the train station gate and you wind up somewhere in Kamurocho's underground mall, or in a building, or even the next station!
When I first got to Tokyo I got lost all the time! It's way too big!
Heh, ain't it just? I still didn't know how to get anywhere when I left to come here.
It's real crowded, ain't it? (Guess that makes it easier for me to get around, though.)
Is it always like this when the snow festival comes around?
Oh, yes. It's a local festival, but for some weird reason, people come from all over to see it.
In Tokyo, it's rare to have snow piles at all. Most of the time it's gone by the next day.
Ah. At work, I get a ton of customers who have come just to see the festival.
I'll bet.
But even as far as locals go, most people only come to look. Only a small few actually make anything.
These days a large portion of the sculptures are made by volunteers who come from outside of Hokkaido.
That's kinda sad. At this rate, the tradition of makin' snow sculptures might wind up dyin' out.
Well, it's hard to make something like what's displayed at the festival, so some people might just make something to put in front of their homes.
Nothin' wrong with that. It's important to keep this kind of tradition goin'.
But ain't there less snow now because of global warming? Ya might not be able to do it in the future. Ain't no better time than the present.
Hehe. You're not even from here, but you're taking it so seriously!
Maybe I ought to make something, too. Hey, maybe I should model a snowman after you, Saejima-san! <Color:255,200,200,255>⑮<Color:Default>
Sounds fun. I wanna see how it comes out.
What do the locals do? This is their festival, after all.
Well most of the folks who do this are professionals. It's not easy for beginners to get in on it.
Yeah, but once there's nobody left to learn the craft from, this'll all be over for good. Ya can't give up on it just 'cause it's hard.
I guess you're right. I wish you lived in Sapporo, Saejima-san.
Hey, why not just become a resident of Sapporo? That would be the most efficient solution!
I do really wanna participate in the festival, but I can't really do that.
Yeah... That's too bad.
Maybe I oughta try. I've shoveled snow in the cold all the time, so it doesn't bother me none.
